message.content: {"thought": "Three fetched sources provide credible limits/challenges to the claim that self-testing beats rereading for long-term retention.", "action": "finish", "args": {"findings": [{"claim": "Across four experiments with different initial test types, problem-solving domains, and participant populations, testing after studying worked examples did not improve delayed problem-solving performance compared to restudy.", "source_id": "W2082988750", "quote": "Thus, across four experiments, with different types of initial tests, different problem-solving domains, and different participant populations, we found no evidence that testing enhanced delayed test performance compared to restudy.", "stance": "challenges"}, {"claim": "In two online Prolific experiments using validated materials, delayed posttests, corrective feedback, and factual plus application measures, retrieval practice produced no significant advantage over restudy at delayed test.", "source_id": "W7125926383", "quote": "No significant differences were found between groups at delayed test, despite multiple safeguards aimed at promoting participant engagement (e.g., prescreening filters, attention checks, fair compensation).", "stance": "limits"}, {"claim": "For briefly encountered academically relevant facts, long-term retention was best when restudy was combined with self-testing rather than replacing restudy with repeated testing.", "source_id": "W4387580672", "quote": "Contrary to prior work, long-term memory was superior for facts the were restudied in addition to self-tested (SST > STT = SSS).", "stance": "limits"}]}}
